Tectonic deformation in the southern part of South China Block: Paleomagnetic
study of the Early Cretaceous Xinlong Formation from Shangsi Foredeep
Depozone in the Guangxi Province
Takuya Kawamuraa, Masayuki Hirotaa, Hiroaki Aokia, Hayao Morinagaa, Yuyan Liub,
Hyeon-Seon Ahnc, Haider Zamand, Masahiko Yokoyamac, Yo-ichiro Otofujic,∗
aDepartment of Global Tectonics, Graduate School of Life Sciences, University of Hyogo, Shosha 2167, Himeji 671-2201, Japan
bFaculty of Earth Science, China University of Geosciences (Wuhan), Yujiashan, Wuhan, China
cDepartment of Earth and Planetary Sciences, Faculty of Science, Kobe University, Kobe, Japan
dDepartment of Geology and Geophysics, College of Science, King Saud University, Riyadh, Saudi Arabia
a r t i c l e i n f o

Keywords:
Tectonics

South China
a

Paleomagnetism
b s t r a c t
To examine tectonic deformation in the southern part of the South China Block, red bed samples have
been collected at 37 sites from the Early Cretaceous Xinlong Formation, south side of the Nanning town
(108.3◦E, 22.8◦N). Stepwise thermal demagnetization and rock magnetic investigations revealed mag-
netite and hematite as the main carriers of remanent magnetizations in the studied samples. Pre-folding
origin for hematite-related magnetic component is supported by positive fold test, whereas a syn-folding
origin is assigned to a component carried by magnetite. A 100% tilt-corrected mean direction for hematite-
related component (Dec/Inc = 3.3◦/41.7◦, k = 43.3, ˛ 95= 4.1◦, N = 29) is considered to have been acquired at
the time of deposition during the Early Cretaceous. Comparison of this direction with previously reported
Cretaceous paleomagnetic directions from the Cathaysia Block (a part of the South China Block) indicates a
gradual increase in counter-clockwise deflected declination toward southwest in this block. The amount
of this counter-clockwise deflection increases up to 13.4◦± 4.7◦ in the southern part of the Cathaysia
Block compared to the stable part of the South China Block. This deflection is ascribed to block rotation as
a result of tectonic deformation in the South China Block during the indentation of India into Asia. Geo-
logical studies and seismic tomographic interpretations suggest that a large degree of counter-clockwise
deflection remained restricted to the Nanpanjiang-Youjiang basin, where low-seismic velocities for both
P and S waves prevail. The presence of mechanically weak crust is considered as a requisite condition for
this rotation in the southern part of the South China Block.
© 2012 Elsevier Ltd. All rights reserved.
1. Introduction
Continental deformation due to collision of India with Asia
can clearly be observed in several parts of Asia, for instance,
around the eastern Himalayan syntaxis in Southeast Asia. As
shown in Fig. 1, a record of cumulative deformational features
is available via the Cretaceous to Eocene paleomagnetic data.
Record of paleomagnetic data from Shan-Thai Block, Indochina
Block, Chuan Dian Fragment and South China Block (SCB) sug-
gest that deformation around the eastern Himalayan syntaxis
is characterized by clockwise (CW) rotations of more than 20◦.
The current direction of continental movement resulting from
crustal deformation is observed by GPS surveys, indicating a
southeast-southward displacement with CW rotation in areas
∗
Corresponding author. Tel.: +81 78 803 5730; fax: +81 78 803 5757.
E-mail address: Otofuji@kobe-u.ac.jp(Y.-i.
around
Otofuji).
eastern Himalayan syntaxes (Allmendinger et al., 2007; Gan
et al., 2007).
However, no significant deformation has been detected in the
SCB by GPS and paleomagnetic observations (Shen et al., 2005;
Vergnolle et al., 2007; Otofuji et al., 2010), except in its south-
western region. The long and slender area between 24◦ and
30◦N latitude and along 103◦E longitude currently undergoes
counter-clockwise (CCW) rotation of more than 2 × 10−8rad/year
(Allmendinger et al., 2007; Gan et al., 2007; Copley, 2008). As indi-
cated in Fig. 1, a CCW rotation up to 20◦ has also been reported
by Gilder et al. (1993) through their paleomagnetic study on the
Early Cretaceous–Early Eocene red beds of the Guanxi Province
(22.5◦N, 108.5◦E), southern part of the SCB. These CCW rotational
motions are in some way peculiar to southern part of the SCB. This
part is located beside the Shan-Thai and Indochina blocks, which
was subjected to southeastward displacement and CW rotation
as a result of Indian Plate indentation in to Asia. It is, there-
fore, predicted that deformation due to collision of India with

Asia might have reached up to as far as the southern part of the
SCB.
Paleomagnetic results from southern part of the SCB can give
us a clue to evaluate the extent of deformation in this region as
a consequence of Indian Plate indentation in to Asia. Because the
reported data from Gilder et al. (1993) suggest a gradual CCW
deflection in declination toward west in and around the Nanning
town, further paleomagnetic investigations were recommended to
obtain reliable data sets. For this purpose, fresh paleomagnetic
samples were collected from the Lower Cretaceous red beds of
the Xinlong Formation. Taking in to consideration the structural
attitude of the area, collection were made from both limbs of the
synclinorium-type structure in the Guangxi Province. As expected,
a paleomagnetic declination change as a function of longitude is
observed in southern part of the SCB, which is then compared with
regional tectono-geological models.
2. Geological setting and sampling
As shown in Fig. 1, amalgamation of the Yangtze Craton with
Cathaysia Block form the SCB, separated by northeast-southwest
trending Neoproterozoic Jiangshan-Shaoxing suture (i.e. Wong
et al., 2011; Yao et al., 2011; Li et al., 2012; Liu et al., 2012). The
Archean basement under the Yangtze Block is covered by Late Pro-
terozoic to Cenozoic sediments (Faure et al., 1996; Wong et al.,
2011), whilst the Proterozoic rocks dominate the basement of
Cathaysia
the
Block (Yao et al., 2011). During the Permian, a deep-
marine embayment (the Yujiang-Nanpanjiang basin) extended
along the southern margin of the SCB from Central Guizhou to Nan-
ning area (Liang and Li, 2005; Lehrmann et al., 2007; Li and Li, 2007).
A western Guangxi fold belt was then formed by tectonic inversion
in the Yujiang-Nanpanjiang basin during the Early to Middle Trias-
sic (Hsu et al., 1988). From Late Triassic to Early Jurassic, most areas
of the SCB underwent comprehensive folding and uplifting, forming
the widely developed Late Triassic–Early Jurassic basins (Shu et al.,
2009). A convex shaped (northwestward directed) foreland fold-
and-thrust belt has been observed in the SCB (Hsu et al., 1988; Li
and Li, 2007), but its timing of formation remained unclear. Follow-
ing this, volcanic-related faulted depressions developed during the
Early Cretaceous. As a result of large scale extensional and crustal
thinning activities during this period, NE-trending grabens were
formed in the eastern part of the SCB (Li, 2000; Ren et al., 2002;
Shu et al., 2009).
As reported in GXBGMR (1985), the Shiwandashan Basin in
the southern part of the Guangxi Province (southeastern part
of the SCB) is one such graben formed sometime between Late
Paleozoic and Cretaceous (Fig. 2a). The central part of this basin
is occupied by the youngest depozone named as Shangsi Fore-
deep Depozone (Liang and Li, 2005), which is filled with Upper
Triassic to Cretaceous sedimentary rocks (Fig. 2a). An angular
unconformity separates the Early Cretaceous red beds from pre-
Jurassic rocks. Layers of fine to coarse-grained red sandstone and

### page_3
42 T. Kawamura et al. / Journal of Geodynamics 64 (2013) 40– 53

insets.
siltstone of the Early Cretaceous Xinlong Formation are exposed
in the Shangsi Foredeep Depozone, southeast of the Nanning area
(108.3◦E, 22.8◦N). Several types of fossils from Early Cretaceous
period (including the pelecypods, vertebrates, plants, ostracods,
estherias, gastropods and charophytes) are identified in the Xin-
long Formation. The Upper Jurassic and Lower Cretaceous red beds
in this basin are gently folded. In case of the Early Cretaceous Xin-
long Formation, the folding activities seem to have occurred soon
after the sedimentary deposition, because a short-lived compres-
sive event of uplifting took place around 100 Ma, mainly in the
coastal areas of the Cathaysia Block (Rowley et al., 1989; Gilder
et al., 1996; Shu et al., 2009).
Paleomagnetic sampling of the Early Cretaceous Xinlong For-
mation were carried out at two localities; one each in the western
and eastern parts of the basin (Fig. 2b). Synclinal structure with
E–W trending axes was observed in the western locality, where
samples from 21 sites (Sites 01–21) were collected along a 30 km
road section. In the eastern part of the basin, samples were col-
lected from synclinorium structure at 16 sites (Sites 22–37).
location
The
of each sampling site was determined by a portable naviga-
tional instrument and paleomagnetic samples were oriented with
magnetic compass. The present declination value at each samp-
ling site was evaluated from International Geomagnetic Reference
Field (International Association of Geomagnetism and Aeronomy
Working Group V-MOD, 2010).
3. Rock magnetic and paleomagnetic procedures
Individual specimens, 25 mm in diameter and 23 mm in length,
were prepared from the collected samples in the laboratory. Natural
remanent magnetizations (NRMs) were measured using a spin-
ner magnetometer (Natsuhara Giken SMM-85). One specimen per
sample was subjected to stepwise thermal demagnetization up
to 690◦C using Natsuhara Giken TDE-91C thermal demagnetizer
with a residual field of less than 5 nT. Demagnetization results for
each specimen were plotted on the orthogonal vector diagrams
(Zijderveld, 1967) to assess component structure of the NRMs as
well as on equal-area projections to evaluate directional stability.

### page_4
T. Kawamura et al. / Journal of Geodynamics 64 (2013) 40– 53 43
Fig. 3. IRM acquisition curves for the representative specimens. Results for western and eastern parts of the study area are shown in (a) and (b), respectively.
Principal component analysis (Kirschvink, 1980) was used to cal-
culate the components directions, while site-mean directions were
calculated using Fisherian statistics (Fisher, 1953).
Progressive acquisitions of isothermal remanent magnetization
(IRM) were performed on the representative specimens up to a
maximum field of 2.7 T using a Magnetic Measurements Pulse Mag-
netizer (MMPM-10). Thermal demagnetization of the composite
IRMs (imparted at 2.7 T, 0.4 T and 0.12 T along z, y and x axes of the
specimens, respectively) was carried out in order to evaluate the
unblocking temperature spectra (Lowrie, 1990). Thermo-magnetic
analyses were conducted on several specimens in air atmosphere
using an automatic recording thermo-magnetic balance at Kyoto
University (with a magnetic field of 0.85 T).
4. The results
4.1. Rock magnetic results
The IRM acquisition curves of the representative samples from
31 out of 37 sites reveal non-achievement of saturation up to a max-
imum field of 2.7 T ((i) and (ii) in Fig. 3), indicating the dominant
presence of high-coercivity magnetic minerals, such as hematite or
goethite. The presence of hematite is then confirmed by unblock-
ing temperature spectra (between 660◦C and 690◦C) of the high
coercive force component (hard component), obtained by thermal
demagnetization of the composite IRMs ((i) and (ii) in Fig. 4).
Samples from the remaining 6 sites (Sites 13, 20, 30, 32, 34 and
35) achieved an IRM saturation up to 2.5 T applied field, suggest-
ing the presence of lower-coercivity magnetic minerals ((iii)
(iv)
and
in Fig. 3). A low coercive force component (soft component)
with weakest IRM intensity is clearly unblocked between 560◦C
and 590◦C, while a hard component is unblocked between 660◦C
and 690◦C ((iii) and (iv) in Fig. 4). These observations on these 6
sites indicate the presence of magnetite and hematite as remanence
carriers. Similar tendency is observed by thermo-magnetic analysis
as well; where two Curie points (580◦C and 670◦C) are observed
in the studied samples (Fig. 5). Heating and cooling phases of the
thermomagnetic curves are not reversible, indicating a conversion
from magnetite to hematite as a result of heating.
4.2. Paleomagnetic results
4.2.1. The NRM intensity
Initial NRM intensities of the studied 246 samples from all sites
range from 6.2 × 10−3 to 8.5 × 10−2A/m. Stronger NRM intensi-
ties are observed in the samples from western part compared to
those from eastern part; i.e. 2.5 ± 1.1 × 10−2A/m (95% confidence
limit) and 1.2 ± 0.4 × 10−2A/m from the western and eastern parts,
respectively.
4.2.2. Demagnetization behavior
Diverse demagnetization behaviors are observed in the stud-
ied samples (Fig. 6). Due to spurious demagnetization behavior
results from a Site 28 are not used in the determination of the
paleomagnetic direction. Two-component behavior is observed in
15 out of 21 sites from western part, whereas three-components
are identified in the remaining sites (including both western
and eastern parts). For a set of sites that carry three magnetic

components, the low, intermediate and high temperature com-

respectively. Combined with rock magnetic results, it can be
concluded that magnetite and hematite are the carriers of
intermediate- and high-temperature components in these samples,
respectively.
4.2.3. The NRM directions
The low-temperature component (LTC) is observed only in 34
out of 246 samples. Directions of this component are distributed
around the present geomagnetic field direction (Fig. 7). An in situ
mean direction calculated for this component (D = 1.8◦, I = 34.8◦,
k = 51.5, ˛ =
95
3.5◦, N = 34) is almost parallel to the geocentric dipole
field (D = 0◦, I = 39.1◦) and the IGRF direction of 2010 (D = 358.3◦,
I = 33.4◦) in the study area. The direction-correction (DC) tilt test
(Enkin, 2003) gives an optimal concentration at 5.7 ± 14.6% unfol-
ding, which is indistinguishable from the corresponding value at
0% unfolding. In the blocking diagrams of Pullaiah et al. (1975),
an unblocking temperature of 350◦C for such a component is
attributed to a relaxation time of about 1 My, during which the
hematite grains acquire a record of the axial geocentric dipole field
at room temperature. The LTC direction is, therefore, considered as
a VRM secondarily-acquired by hematite grains during the Bruhnes
Chron.
Since the intermediate and high temperature components are
expectedly carried by magnetite and hematite, respectively, rema-
nent directions for these components are calculated separately.
These intermediate (between 350◦C and 590◦C) and high tem-
perature (590◦C and 690◦C) components are identified in 35 and
31 sites, respectively. Because large ˛ values
95
(17.5◦or more) are
observed in two of the studied sites (Sites 09 and 36), their results
are not used in the calculation of formation mean

direction.

In case of high-temperature component the evidences point to
its pre-folding origin. When the DC tilt test (Enkin, 2003) is applied
to 29 out of 31 sites for the high-temperature component, an opti-
mal concentration is attained at 72.4 ± 22.0% unfolding (Fig. 8).
However, when a separate fold test is applied to 17 sites from west-
ern part, where the Early Cretaceous Xinlong Formation forms a
typical anticlinal structure, an optimal concentration reaches up to
88.3 ± 24.2% unfolding, indicating a pre-folding origin. Compared
to this, an optimal concentration is attained at 61.0 ± 37.2% unfol-
ding for the remaining 12 sites from eastern part. This divergent
behavior is probably due to variable striking attitudes within the
eastern part, where some local-scale heterogeneous deformation
might have occurred. Because beddings in the area are dominantly
characterized by NW–SE directed strikes, two data sites from west-
ward dipping strata (Sites 31 and 35) and eight from eastward
dipping strata (Sites 22, 23, 24, 25, 30, 32, 34 and 35) were selected
for another fold test. This technique has been proposed both by
McFadden’s (1990) and Cogné (2003) to examine the fold test via
first definition ((cid:2) ).
1
When applied to our data, a value of 4.431
is obtained for (cid:2) in
1
the geographic coordinates and 2.767 in the
stratigraphic coordinates, whilst a critical value ((cid:2)c) of 3.865 is
calculated all at 95% confidence level. The selected data sets from
eastern part thus passed the fold test. Based on these estimations,
the high-temperature component, both from western and east-
ern parts of the basin, is declared as pre-fold in origin, and the
formation mean direction at 100% un-tilting (Dec/Inc = 3.3◦/40.2◦,
k = 43.3, ˛ =
95
4.1◦, N = 29) is considered as the characteristic rema-
nent magnetization (ChRM) direction for the Xinlong Formation in
the studied basin (see Table 1a).
A syn-folding origin is inferred for the intermediate-
temperature NRM component. Based on the calculation for
33 sites, this magnetite related component shows an attainment of
optimal concentration at 54.0 ± 15.1% unfolding. Separate fold tests
for the western and eastern parts indicate optimal concentrations
at 53.1 ± 16.7% and 56.0 ± 27.0% unfolding, respectively. These
observations thus favor a syn-folding origin for the intermediate-
temperature component. A mean direction of Dec/Inc = 1.5/44.1◦
(k = 72.6, ˛ =
95
3.0◦, N = 33) is obtained for this component at 54%
unfolding (Table 1b)
4.2.4. Evaluation of the results
4.2.4.1. Declination. Because the western and eastern parts of the
study area are separated by more than 40 km, paleomagnetic
directions at 100% unfolding for the high-temperature component
are compared to examine areal variation. Although mean incli-
nations from both these parts are nearly identical (Iwest= 40.9◦
versus Ieast= 39.1◦), declination in the western part is more westerly
deflected compared to the eastern part. A plot of declinations versus
longitudes for Nanning area is given in Fig. 9A, where an increase in
westerly deflected declinations is indicated when moving toward
west. The observed declinations in the western and eastern parts
vary from −18◦to 14◦and −10◦to 31◦, respectively. Their formation
mean declinations are Dwest= 358.1◦ (˛ =
95
3.7◦) and Deast= 10.8◦
(˛ =
95
9.0◦), respectively. The largest easterly deflected declina-
tions (Deastern most area= 18–27◦) are observed at three sites (Sites
22–24) in the easternmost margin of the eastern part. Almost
similar tendency is observed in the paleomagnetic directions

reliability of both these components, 27 sites were selected
for this purpose. Nineteen among 27 sites reveal sallower
inclinations for the high-temperature component at 100%
unfolding than that of the intermediate-temperature compo-
nent at 54% unfolding (I
high temperature
=
component

I
intermediate temperature
=

(e.g. Mandel, 1964) to arithmetic mean inclinations from 27 sites
indicates a significant statistical difference between these two com-
ponents at 95% confidence level.
5. Discussion and interpretation
5.1. Hematite and magnetite related magnetizations
NRMs in the studied red beds are discriminated on the basis
of magnetite and hematite as carriers of intermediate- and high-
temperature components. Application of fold test indicates a
pre-folding origin for hematite-related component, whereas a syn-
folding origin is predicted for magnetite related component. It is,
therefore, concluded that the component of magnetization carried
by hematite is an earlier record of geomagnetic field compared to
that carried by magnetite.
Syn-folding origin for magnetite related component could be
explained in the light of different magnetization processes. One
of the possible processes is the acquisition of chemical remanent
magnetization (CRM) by secondary magnetite during the folding
episode. Formation of magnetite from soils and sulfide-rich mud is
reported by some researchers (Maher and Taylor, 1988; Sakaguchi
et al., 1993), while laboratory based dehydration of goethite in
to magnetite is observed by others (Ozdemir and Dunlop, 2000).
On the other hand, alteration of pre-existing pyrite to authigenic
magnetite is reported by Suk et al. (1990). Because formation of
magnetite is an inevitable phenomenon in nature, its secondary
occurrence with attendant CRM component is very much pos-
sible during folding. An alternative possibility is the process of
post-depositional remanent magnetization (pDRM) of primarily
deposited magnetite grains. It should be noted that there are dif-
ferent cessation times for hematite and magnetite grains in the
interstices of non-magnetic minerals. Because the hematite grains
are disk shaped crystals (specularite), they can easily get fixed in
wet sedimentary layers after deposition prior to folding activities.
In contrast, magnetite grains are isometric in shape, so capable of
rotating even long after the hematite grains locking and can con-
tinue until the time of folding. Another possibility is re-rotation
of magnetite grains due to reactivation of pDRM processes during
folding when fluids get into the lithified layers through structurally-
controlled pathways (Ghisetti and Vezzani, 2000).
Paleomagnetic direction of the magnetite-related component
at 54% unfolding is thus recognized to have acquired long after
the initial deposition of the Early Cretaceous Xinlong Formation.
Steeper inclination for this component is either attributed to tem-
poral variation of the geomagnetic field or to post-depositional
tectonic processes, because its acquisition through CRM or pDRM
is generally free from shallowing effect as in the case hematite-
related magnetization. Further study is needed to properly address
this issue of syn-folding acquisition in magnetite grains.

of the area. Moving from 109.8◦E to 108.3◦E longitudes (westward)
in the Guangxi Province and incorporating the previously-reported
Cretaceous to Eocene paleomagnetic data from Xinlong Formation
(Gilder et al., 1993), a gradual increase in CCW deflection in dec-
lination is observed toward west (Fig. 9B). As shown in Fig. 9B,
a relatively large CCW deflected declination appears in the west-
ern most part (the Youjiang Basin), where a maximum value up to
D = 325.5◦ is reported from the Paleocene-Lower Eocene red beds
(Gilder et al., 1993). A gradual increase of declination in this region
is further viewed in the distribution of three pole positions (Fig. 10).
Compilation of the Cretaceous paleomagnetic data from Cathaysia
Block (Table 2) enables us to confirm this behavior (Fig. 9C) within
an area located between the central part of the Cathaysia Block
and the Guanxi province, including the Nanning area. An arithmetic
mean of declination from 121◦E to 114◦E longitudes reveals a small
CW deflection (D = 14.2◦± 6.7◦). These observations thus suggest
that a CCW deflection in declination gradually increases toward the
southwest when moving away from central part of the Cathaysia
Block.
This spatial change in declination within the Cathaysia Block
could be attributed to regional tectonic deformation. The effects of
geomagnetic filed and APWP could not be the reason here, because
the Cretaceous paleomagnetic data related to Cathaysia Block have
been obtained from the red beds, in which the short term geomag-
netic secular variations are adequately averaged out, and the APWP
of Eurasia have no record of such a large shift during the Creta-
ceous period (Besse and Courtillot, 2002). It thus seems reasonable
to declare that tectonic activities are the cause of spatial declination
change in the southern part of the SCB.
The Nanning area was subjected to CCW tectonic rotation of
13.4◦± 4.7◦ with respect to the stable part of the SCB, compared
with the expected direction calculated from the Cretaceous paleo-
magnetic pole for the stable part of the SCB. The Mesozoic thrust
fault and fold belts in the SCB indicate a convex shape structure
with northwestward trend (Fig. 1). As a first-order approximation,
the axes of these trends in the SCB are about N–S in the west-
ern part (the Guangxi fold belt), NE–SW in the central part and
E–W in the northern part. Based on the paleomagnetic data from
Permo-Triassic rocks (Steiner et al., 1989; Huang and Opdyke, 1996;
Tan et al., 2007), oroclinal bending is suggested for the origin of
this curvature in the northern part of the belt. Because the cur-
vature formation in the southern part of this belt could partly be
explained by oroclinal bending, a CCW rotational motion around
the Nanning area is possibly a reflection of the SCB scale tectonic
deformation.
5.3. Tectonic deformation in the southern part of the SCB
The present study claims that the CCW rotation in the southern
part of the SCB occurred after the deposition of the Early Creta-
ceous Xinlong Formation. Two phases of large tectonic events are
recognized in the SCB; the Mesozoic collision between the North
China Block (NCB) and the SCB, and the Early Cenozoic shortening
in the SCB and Tibet as a result of India-Asia collision (e.g. Gilder
et al., 1999). These observations suggest that CCW rotation in the
southern part of the SCB occurred during the second phase.
Following the pioneering work of Tapponnier et al. (1982), sev-
eral tectonic models have been presented to understand the aspects
of deformation in the Asian continent due to its collision with India.
According to recently reported model (Cook and Royden, 2008),
small amount of CCW rotation is revealed in the southern part of
the SCB. Whilst this model requires an eastward directed
crustal
lower
flow as a result of India-Asia collision, heterogeneity of the
upper crust is required; means strong crust in the Sichuan Basin and
weak crust in the southern part of the SCB. Because other reported
models assume a uniform strength (homogeneity) for the litho-
sphere under the Asian Continent (Tapponnier et al., 1982; Peltzer
and Tapponnier, 1988; Houseman and England, 1986, 1993), only
CW rotation is predicted for the blocks located in the east of the
indenting Indian Plate. The present study and its comparison with
others thus suggest a weak crust as a requisite condition for CCW
rotation in the southern part of the SCB.
Deformation of the lithosphere is generally linked to age of the
tectonic blocks, as mechanical strength of the lithosphere increases
with age (Simon and van der Hilst, 2002; Perez-Gussinye and Watts,
2005). The presence of weak crust is expected beneath the south-
ern part of the SCB because a post-Triassic fold belt has now been
recognized in this region. The northern part of the SCB consists of
the Archean to Proteorzoic Yangtze Craton and the Cathaysia Block,
whereas its southern part has been re-demarcated as a western
Guangxi fold belt (Hsu et al., 1988) formed as a result of tectonic
inversion in the Yujiang-Nanpanjiang basin (Fig. 1). This basin had
an extension from Central Guizhou to Nanning area during the
Permian that later evolved into a foreland basin during the Early
to Middle Triassic (Liang and Li, 2005; Lehrmann et al., 2007; Li and
Li, 2007). Basin formation and inversion tectonics could be taken
as a clue for reduced upper crustal strength in the southern part of
the SCB.
Lateral variation in mechanical strength within the SCB is also
demonstrated by seismic tomography results (Lebedev and Nolet,
2003; Li et al., 2006, 2008; An and Shi, 2006). The Yangtze Block,
which is located to the northwest of the Yujiang-Nanpanjiang basin,
is characterized by high velocity P-wave propagation up to 250-km
deep (Li et al., 2006, 2008). This type of seismic behavior indi-
cates a deep rooted and mechanically stiff tectonic unit underlain
by craton-like lithosphere. In contrast, major part of the Cathaysia
Block is characterized by moderate P wave velocity in addition to
low velocities (both P and S waves) zones in the southern part.
These observations thus suggest that lithospheric strength beneath
the southern part of the Cathaysia Block is relatively weaker than
that of the northern part, and much lower than that of the Yangtze
Craton, implying a non-uniform or heterogeneous nature of the
SCB.
6. Conclusions
1. Two magnetization components, carried by hematite and mag-
netite, have been discriminated in the Lower Cretaceous red
beds of the Xinlong Formation, south side of the Nanning town
(108.3◦E, 22.8◦N). The hematite related component is deter-
mined as pre-folding in origin, whereas a syn-folding origin is
assigned to magnetite related component.
2. The formation mean direction at 100% un-tilting for the
hematite-related magnetization component (Dec/Inc = 3.3◦/
40.2◦, k = 43.3, ˛ = 95 4.1◦, N = 29) represents a ChRM for the Early
Cretaceous period in the Nanning area. Based on the directions
of this component, westerly deflected declination is observed in
the western part (D = 358.1◦) of the study area compared to its
eastern part (D = 10.8◦).
3. An integrated paleomagnetic database of the previous and
present studies depicts a gradual increase in CCW deflection
when moving toward southwest in the Cathaysia Block.
4. This increase in CCW deflection was most likely caused by
regional tectonic deformation experienced by the southern part
of the SCB. As a result of this deformation, the studied Nanning
area underwent up to 13.4◦± 4.7◦CCW rotation with respect to
stable part of the SCB.

### page_13
52 T. Kawamura et al. / Journal of Geodynamics 64 (2013) 40– 53
5. Regional scale CCW rotation in the southern part of the SCB is
attributed to mechanically weak lithosphere under the area, as
confirmed by geological and seismic tomography results from
the area.
